content_html:
You need to tread carefully among the leaf litter of the Indonesian scrubland and its tropical rainforests. The dead leaves might seem caught in a gentle breeze, but there's more here than meets the eye. Try plucking one from the ground and you'll find an insect caught in the act of prayer.

Not a leaf, but a dead leaf mantis.

Dead leaf mantises are a marvel, their thorax sculpted by evolution to mimic the veins of dying vegetation. This clever act of camouflage helps them hide from predators and ambush prey.

Kris Anderson, an independent researcher and mantis specialist, has seen more than his fair share of this genus, known as Deroplatys, in his decades collecting and categorizing Mantodea, the order of insects that includes all mantises.

A new species recently caught his eye. As he browsed the citizen science platform iNaturalist—where he's made more than 26,000 identifications—he came across a user-submitted image of a Deroplatys. The user claimed it was discovered in a tropical forest in Malaysia.

This particular specimen rested vertically on a branch, clinging with its hind legs—a diamond-shaped faux leaf suspended like a shield over its body. While it had all the features of a dead leaf mantis, some inconsistencies caught Anderson's well-trained eye. The shape of its head, its antennae and the patterns that rippled across its body were all features he hadn't seen before.

These inconsistencies were evidence of a deeper, more concerning truth: This mantis does not exist. It's a fabrication, created with generative AI image tools.

As these tools improve, biodiversity platforms reliant on citizen science, such as iNaturalist and eBird, may see increasing numbers of fakes and fraudulent depictions that are much harder to detect.

Anderson has written twice about fake mantises in the past 6 months, sparked by entries on iNaturalist. He's concerned the problem could spiral and that fake observations might even appear in scientific papers, surveys and environmental assessments without adequate verification processes in place.

"Because so much modern biodiversity research increasingly incorporates citizen science records, I felt it was important to document this vulnerability early, before AI-generated observations became commonplace," says Anderson.

However, there are already signs the AI-slopification of citizen science has arrived.

Tit for tat

In November 2025, descriptions of a willow tit in northeast Scotland captivated twitchers on social media. The tit, a palm-sized perching bird with a helmet of black feathers, is an extremely rare find.

And yet, in an image uploaded to a Scottish birding site, one seemed to be sticking its tiny beak into a bird feeder.

When Alexander Lees inspected the photo, he broke into a cold sweat. He noticed the bird's deformed feet and beak and identified the image as a fake. A reader in biodiversity and bird specialist at Manchester Metropolitan University in England, Lees has been uncovering more and more AI slop on citizen science platforms.

Those platforms have been crucial for his research—he's published on everything from bird migration to the colors of woodpecker plumage based on observational data uploaded to these services.

In early July, he wrote an opinion piece published in Nature Ecology & Evolution alongside staff from iNaturalist, outlining how these databases could become "contaminated" by AI-generated data fabrication and public misinformation.

The willow tit was an extreme example—one in which an entire animal was generated wholly by code—and was almost convincing enough to fool some "ornithologists," according to Lees. But AI doesn't need to create whole observations to contaminate the scientific record—enhancements could also prove problematic.

"Problems with denoising and 'beautifying' existing imagery are likely much [more common] than people trying to pass off entirely AI-generated imagery as a biological record, but both are highly problematic," Lees says.

In their paper, Lees and his team showed how easy it might be to generate a fake. They asked Gemini, the Google-backed chatbot, to generate an image of a red-winged blackbird on a branch backed by a blue sky. The result was fairly convincing, aside from an odd-looking number of tail feathers.

They also took an image of an oriole native to South America and asked Gemini to "make this look better." The image crafted by the AI seemed to add a red flare to the oriole's wing, which led the team to suggest it might fool an expert ornithologist or computer-vision classifiers as a bona fide example of a red-winged blackbird.

This recently happened—innocently—on iNaturalist. A user had touched up an image in this same way, which led to the first description of the red-winged blackbird in Brazil. This was detected, and the image was hidden from the database.

A history of hoaxes

The wings of the Charlton brimstone sparkle a vibrant yellow in the sun, marked only by two bold blue moons, one on each wing. The butterfly was first described in the early 1700s by James Petiver, a London-based chemist, after he was gifted the spectacular lepidopteran by a friend, William Charlton.

By 1763, the species had made its way into the scientific literature, appearing as one of the 100 invertebrates listed in the Centuria Insectorum Rariorum, a book penned by the father of modern biological classification, Carl Linnaeus.

The specimen handed to Petiver remained at the British Museum throughout the 18th century, until it was inspected by Johann Christian Fabricius, a Danish insect specialist. Fabricius noted the two blue moons on the wings were not a mark of a species' long evolution.

They were marks made on the wings of a common brimstone by human hands. The Charlton brimstone did not exist.

While it remains unclear if this was a deliberate deception (reports suggest a curator at the British Museum was so incensed with the fake that he stamped it to dust) or a simple prank gone awry, it highlights how hoaxes have long been a part of identifying and examining species—and their impact on the scientific record.

"Data quality is an issue in biodiversity data that predates electronic data and even computers, let alone AI," said a spokesperson for the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA). The ALA is a digital, open infrastructure that pulls together biodiversity data from across the country—and sometimes the mythic and the fantastic have slipped into the database.

"Like most data managers, the Atlas of Living Australia has seen its fair share of unicorns, tyrannosaurs and anonymous lovers submitted, which have been filtered out."

Artificial intelligence is a force multiplier. Generative tools make it simple to perpetrate these kinds of forgeries. The tools are readily available to anyone who has the time to do so. On social media, fake species have proliferated at pace, usually accompanied by AI-generated descriptions about their behaviors and habitats. Often, the responses are credulous, believing the images to be real.

A community of spies

While citizen science platforms are vulnerable to AI-generated submissions, their communities are full of committed and honest contributors following their passion or looking to make a difference. These members are discerning and dedicated.

"There are lots of really capable reviewers and contributors out there that give vast amounts of their time to maintain the integrity of databases," says Lees. "I suspect we will need a helping hand with toolkits to flag potentially problematic records," he adds.

For iNaturalist, which houses some 500 million images, the threat of fakes isn't new. It has battled against Photoshopped images and erroneous records that use images obtained from elsewhere on the internet. Things are moving fast, and iNaturalist knows it must move quickly too.

"As AI tools become more accessible and the tech landscape shifts, we're working to adapt while keeping scientific integrity at the heart of what we do," an iNaturalist spokesperson told Particle.

To combat the potential for AI-generated chicanery, the spokesperson noted the recent addition of community tools that flag AI-generated content in an effort to maintain the reliability of the biodiversity data on iNaturalist.

Anderson, the mantis expert, is convinced that the scientific literature will eventually experience its own case of AI-generated fakery. Lees agrees, saying "it would be easy to claim a discovery" and suggesting that, if this trickery is knowingly performed by scientists, it would certainly be a case of misconduct and fraud.

"Let's hope this doesn't happen," says Lees.

That ecologists, conservationists and citizen science platforms are experiencing a rise in generative AI alongside the dual crises of climate change and biodiversity loss is deeply concerning. But a third crisis envelops taxonomy—the science of classifying species. There aren't enough experts describing and cataloging species.

While the runaway train of generative AI is yet to crash into this triple crisis, it's not a stretch to consider how ever-improving AI image models could soon produce such imperceptible distinctions between reality and fantasy that even the most discerning experts will struggle to tell the difference. How do we fight back?

Countermeasures

There are three aspects to countering the rise of AI in these spaces, according to Lees. They suggest citizen science platforms should have robust image-authentication protocols and metadata checks to ensure imagery uploaded is a legitimate observation.

A bigger piece is ensuring those using AI tools and citizen science platforms are aware of the pitfalls of the systems they're using. "Given that a big part of the problem is the public adoption of a new technology, education about the problems this causes will hopefully help," says Lees.

While there is a strong desire to keep AI slop out of citizen science platforms, there are instances where AI and machine learning models may be beneficial to conservation and biodiversity efforts. "AI brings new challenges but also potentially new solutions," says the ALA spokesperson.

Using eBird data, an AI model predicted bird migration patterns weeks before the birds got on the move. The CitClops project, a citizen science project that asks members of the public to take photos of seawater, used AI to monitor early signs of algal blooms.

And in Australia, machine learning systems—which work differently from the generative AI systems creating fakes—have recently been used by the Australian Wildlife Conservancy to interpret imagery from camera traps. This AI has been trained on more than 1.1 million images of wildlife (which were also vetted by a real human). That enables it to pick out, for instance, an emu or a wallaby, greatly reducing the manual labor of checking the camera traps. And, notably, species classification isn't a role for the AI. The AI helps group imagery into a data set, and humans verify the work.

It's that element—us—that appears to be key to any resistance we might mount against the explosion of misinformation and forgery that generative AI enables. It is the passionate and dedicated contributors and curators of citizen science platforms who are, so far, proving to be the best defense against the invasion of the slop.

blocks.html_en: "Because so much modern biodiversity research increasingly incorporates citizen science records, I felt it was important to document this vulnerability early, before AI-generated observations became commonplace," says Anderson.

sentences.en: The tit, a palm-sized perching bird with a helmet of black feathers, is an extremely rare find.

blocks.html_en: Those platforms have been crucial for his research—he's published on everything from bird migration to the colors of woodpecker plumage based on observational data uploaded to these services.

sentences.en: Those platforms have been crucial for his research—he's published on everything from bird migration to the colors of woodpecker plumage based on observational data uploaded to these services.

blocks.html_en: In early July, he wrote an opinion piece published in Nature Ecology & Evolution alongside staff from iNaturalist, outlining how these databases could become "contaminated" by AI-generated data fabrication and public misinformation.

sentences.en: In early July, he wrote an opinion piece published in Nature Ecology & Evolution alongside staff from iNaturalist, outlining how these databases could become "contaminated" by AI-generated data fabrication and public misinformation.

blocks.html_en: "Problems with denoising and 'beautifying' existing imagery are likely much [more common] than people trying to pass off entirely AI-generated imagery as a biological record, but both are highly problematic," Lees says.

sentences.en: "Problems with denoising and 'beautifying' existing imagery are likely much [more common] than people trying to pass off entirely AI-generated imagery as a biological record, but both are highly problematic," Lees says.

sentences.en: They asked Gemini, the Google-backed chatbot, to generate an image of a red-winged blackbird on a branch backed by a blue sky.

sentences.en: The image crafted by the AI seemed to add a red flare to the oriole's wing, which led the team to suggest it might fool an expert ornithologist or computer-vision classifiers as a bona fide example of a red-winged blackbird.
sentences.zh: 人工智能制作的图像似乎为黄莺的翅膀添加了红色耀斑，这使得研究小组认为它可能会欺骗鸟类学家或计算机视觉分类器，将其视为红翅黑鸟的真实例子。

blocks.html_en: This recently happened—innocently—on iNaturalist. A user had touched up an image in this same way, which led to the first description of the red-winged blackbird in Brazil. This was detected, and the image was hidden from the database.

sentences.zh: 一位用户以同样的方式修改了图像，从而产生了对巴西红翅黑鸟的第一个描述。

sentences.en: A history of hoaxes
sentences.zh: 恶作剧的历史

blocks.html_en: The wings of the Charlton brimstone sparkle a vibrant yellow in the sun, marked only by two bold blue moons, one on each wing. The butterfly was first described in the early 1700s by James Petiver, a London-based chemist, after he was gifted the spectacular lepidopteran by a friend, William Charlton.

sentences.en: The wings of the Charlton brimstone sparkle a vibrant yellow in the sun, marked only by two bold blue moons, one on each wing.
sentences.zh: 查尔顿硫磺的翅膀在阳光下闪烁着鲜艳的黄色，只有两个大胆的蓝色月亮，每个翅膀上都有一个。

sentences.en: The butterfly was first described in the early 1700s by James Petiver, a London-based chemist, after he was gifted the spectacular lepidopteran by a friend, William Charlton.
sentences.zh: 1700 年代初，伦敦化学家詹姆斯·佩蒂弗 (James Petiver) 的朋友威廉·查尔顿 (William Charlton) 送给他这种壮观的鳞翅目昆虫，并首次描述了这种蝴蝶。

blocks.html_en: By 1763, the species had made its way into the scientific literature, appearing as one of the 100 invertebrates listed in the Centuria Insectorum Rariorum, a book penned by the father of modern biological classification, Carl Linnaeus.

sentences.en: By 1763, the species had made its way into the scientific literature, appearing as one of the 100 invertebrates listed in the Centuria Insectorum Rariorum, a book penned by the father of modern biological classification, Carl Linnaeus.
sentences.zh: 到 1763 年，该物种已进入科学文献，作为现代生物分类之父卡尔·林奈 (Carl Linnaeus) 撰写的《Centuria Insectorum Rariorum》中列出的 100 种无脊椎动物之一。

blocks.html_en: The specimen handed to Petiver remained at the British Museum throughout the 18th century, until it was inspected by Johann Christian Fabricius, a Danish insect specialist. Fabricius noted the two blue moons on the wings were not a mark of a species' long evolution.

sentences.en: The specimen handed to Petiver remained at the British Museum throughout the 18th century, until it was inspected by Johann Christian Fabricius, a Danish insect specialist.
sentences.zh: 交给佩蒂弗的标本在整个 18 世纪一直保存在大英博物馆，直到丹麦昆虫专家约翰·克里斯蒂安·法布里修斯 (Johann Christian Fabricius) 对它进行了检查。

sentences.en: Fabricius noted the two blue moons on the wings were not a mark of a species' long evolution.
sentences.zh: 法布里修斯指出，翅膀上的两个蓝色月亮并不是一个物种长期进化的标志。

blocks.html_en: They were marks made on the wings of a common brimstone by human hands. The Charlton brimstone did not exist.

sentences.en: They were marks made on the wings of a common brimstone by human hands.
sentences.zh: 它们是人类双手在普通硫磺翅膀上留下的痕迹。

sentences.en: The Charlton brimstone did not exist.
sentences.zh: 查尔顿硫磺并不存在。

blocks.html_en: While it remains unclear if this was a deliberate deception (reports suggest a curator at the British Museum was so incensed with the fake that he stamped it to dust) or a simple prank gone awry, it highlights how hoaxes have long been a part of identifying and examining species—and their impact on the scientific record.

sentences.en: While it remains unclear if this was a deliberate deception (reports suggest a curator at the British Museum was so incensed with the fake that he stamped it to dust) or a simple prank gone awry, it highlights how hoaxes have long been a part of identifying and examining species—and their impact on the scientific record.
sentences.zh: 虽然目前还不清楚这是否是一次故意的欺骗（有报道称，大英博物馆的一位馆长对假货非常愤怒，以至于将其踩成了灰尘）还是一个简单的恶作剧，但它突显了恶作剧长期以来一直是识别和检查物种的一部分，以及它们对科学记录的影响。

sentences.en: "Data quality is an issue in biodiversity data that predates electronic data and even computers, let alone AI," said a spokesperson for the Atlas of Living Australia (ALA).
sentences.zh: 澳大利亚生活地图集 (ALA) 的发言人表示：“数据质量是生物多样性数据中的一个问题，早于电子数据甚至计算机，更不用说人工智能了。”

blocks.html_en: "Like most data managers, the Atlas of Living Australia has seen its fair share of unicorns, tyrannosaurs and anonymous lovers submitted, which have been filtered out."

sentences.en: "Like most data managers, the Atlas of Living Australia has seen its fair share of unicorns, tyrannosaurs and anonymous lovers submitted, which have been filtered out."
sentences.zh: “像大多数数据管理人员一样，《澳大利亚生活地图集》中提交了相当多的独角兽、霸王龙和匿名恋人，但这些都已被过滤掉。”

sentences.en: Artificial intelligence is a force multiplier.

sentences.en: Generative tools make it simple to perpetrate these kinds of forgeries.

blocks.html_en: A community of spies

sentences.en: A community of spies
sentences.zh: 间谍社区

blocks.html_en: While citizen science platforms are vulnerable to AI-generated submissions, their communities are full of committed and honest contributors following their passion or looking to make a difference. These members are discerning and dedicated.

sentences.en: While citizen science platforms are vulnerable to AI-generated submissions, their communities are full of committed and honest contributors following their passion or looking to make a difference.
sentences.zh: 虽然公民科学平台很容易受到人工智能生成的提交内容的影响，但他们的社区充满了忠诚而诚实的贡献者，他们追随自己的热情或寻求做出改变。

sentences.en: These members are discerning and dedicated.
sentences.zh: 这些成员具有敏锐的洞察力和奉献精神。

blocks.html_en: "There are lots of really capable reviewers and contributors out there that give vast amounts of their time to maintain the integrity of databases," says Lees. "I suspect we will need a helping hand with toolkits to flag potentially problematic records," he adds.

sentences.en: "There are lots of really capable reviewers and contributors out there that give vast amounts of their time to maintain the integrity of databases," says Lees.

sentences.zh: “我怀疑我们需要工具包来标记可能有问题的记录，”他补充道。

blocks.html_en: For iNaturalist, which houses some 500 million images, the threat of fakes isn't new. It has battled against Photoshopped images and erroneous records that use images obtained from elsewhere on the internet. Things are moving fast, and iNaturalist knows it must move quickly too.

sentences.en: For iNaturalist, which houses some 500 million images, the threat of fakes isn't new.
sentences.zh: 对于拥有约 5 亿张图像的 iNaturalist 来说，假货的威胁并不新鲜。

sentences.en: It has battled against Photoshopped images and erroneous records that use images obtained from elsewhere on the internet.
sentences.zh: 它一直在与 Photoshop 图像和使用从互联网其他地方获得的图像的错误记录进行斗争。

blocks.html_en: "As AI tools become more accessible and the tech landscape shifts, we're working to adapt while keeping scientific integrity at the heart of what we do," an iNaturalist spokesperson told Particle.

sentences.en: "As AI tools become more accessible and the tech landscape shifts, we're working to adapt while keeping scientific integrity at the heart of what we do," an iNaturalist spokesperson told Particle.
sentences.zh: iNaturalist 发言人告诉 Particle：“随着人工智能工具变得越来越容易使用以及技术格局发生变化，我们正在努力适应，同时将科学完整性作为我们工作的核心。”

blocks.html_en: To combat the potential for AI-generated chicanery, the spokesperson noted the recent addition of community tools that flag AI-generated content in an effort to maintain the reliability of the biodiversity data on iNaturalist.

sentences.en: To combat the potential for AI-generated chicanery, the spokesperson noted the recent addition of community tools that flag AI-generated content in an effort to maintain the reliability of the biodiversity data on iNaturalist.
sentences.zh: 为了打击人工智能生成的欺诈行为，发言人指出，最近添加了标记人工智能生成内容的社区工具，以维护 iNaturalist 上生物多样性数据的可靠性。

sentences.en: Anderson, the mantis expert, is convinced that the scientific literature will eventually experience its own case of AI-generated fakery.

sentences.en: Lees agrees, saying "it would be easy to claim a discovery" and suggesting that, if this trickery is knowingly performed by scientists, it would certainly be a case of misconduct and fraud.
sentences.zh: 利斯对此表示同意，他说“声称有一项发现是很容易的”，并暗示，如果科学家故意进行这种欺骗，那么这肯定是一种不当行为和欺诈。

sentences.en: That ecologists, conservationists and citizen science platforms are experiencing a rise in generative AI alongside the dual crises of climate change and biodiversity loss is deeply concerning.

sentences.en: But a third crisis envelops taxonomy—the science of classifying species.

blocks.html_en: Countermeasures

sentences.en: Countermeasures
sentences.zh: 对策

blocks.html_en: There are three aspects to countering the rise of AI in these spaces, according to Lees. They suggest citizen science platforms should have robust image-authentication protocols and metadata checks to ensure imagery uploaded is a legitimate observation.

sentences.en: There are three aspects to countering the rise of AI in these spaces, according to Lees.

sentences.en: They suggest citizen science platforms should have robust image-authentication protocols and metadata checks to ensure imagery uploaded is a legitimate observation.
sentences.zh: 他们建议公民科学平台应该拥有强大的图像验证协议和元数据检查，以确保上传的图像是合法的观察结果。

sentences.en: A bigger piece is ensuring those using AI tools and citizen science platforms are aware of the pitfalls of the systems they're using.

content_html_zh:
您需要在印度尼西亚灌木丛及其热带雨林的落叶层中小心行走。 枯叶似乎被微风吹拂，但这里的东西远比表面上看到的要多。 尝试从地上拔出一只，你会发现一只正在祈祷的昆虫。

不是一片叶子，而是一只死叶螳螂。

枯叶螳螂是一个奇迹，它们的胸部经过进化而雕刻而成，模仿垂死植物的静脉。 这种巧妙的伪装行为可以帮助它们躲避掠食者和伏击猎物。

克里斯·安德森 (Kris Anderson) 是一位独立研究员和螳螂专家，在他数十年对螳螂目（包括所有螳螂的昆虫纲）的收集和分类中，对这种被称为 Deroplatys 的属的了解超出了他应有的份额。

最近，一个新物种引起了他的注意。 当他浏览公民科学平台 iNaturalist 时（他在该平台上进行了 26,000 多次识别），他发现了一张用户提交的 Deroplatys 图像。 该用户声称它是在马来西亚的热带森林中发现的。

这个特殊的标本垂直地停在树枝上，用后腿紧贴着它——一块菱形的人造叶子像盾牌一样悬挂在它的身体上。 虽然它具有枯叶螳螂的所有特征，但一些不一致之处吸引了安德森训练有素的眼睛。 它的头部形状、触角以及全身波纹状的图案，都是他以前从未见过的特征。

这些不一致之处证明了一个更深刻、更令人担忧的事实：这只螳螂并不存在。 这是一个用生成人工智能图像工具创建的虚构作品。

随着这些工具的改进，依赖公民科学的生物多样性平台（例如 iNaturalist 和 eBird）可能会看到越来越多的伪造品和欺诈性描述，而且这些描述更难被发现。

在 iNaturalist 上的条目的推动下，安德森在过去 6 个月里写了两篇有关假螳螂的文章。 他担心问题可能会愈演愈烈，如果没有适当的验证程序，虚假的观察结果甚至可能出现在科学论文、调查和环境评估中。

安德森说：“由于现代生物多样性研究越来越多地纳入公民科学记录，我认为在人工智能生成的观察结果变得普遍之前尽早记录这种脆弱性非常重要。”

然而，已有迹象表明公民科学的人工智能倾斜已经到来。

以牙还牙

2025 年 11 月，对苏格兰东北部一只柳树山雀的描述在社交媒体上吸引了推特用户。 山雀是一种手掌大小的栖息鸟类，戴着黑色羽毛的头盔，是一种极其罕见的发现。

然而，在上传到苏格兰观鸟网站的一张图像中，一只鸟似乎将它的小喙伸进了喂鸟器中。

当亚历山大·李斯检查照片时，他出了一身冷汗。 他注意到这只鸟的脚和喙变形了，并认定该图像是赝品。 作为英国曼彻斯特城市大学生物多样性和鸟类专家的读者，李斯在公民科学平台上发现了越来越多的人工智能漏洞。

这些平台对他的研究至关重要——他根据上传到这些服务的观测数据发表了从鸟类迁徙到啄木鸟羽毛颜色的各种内容。

7 月初，他与 iNaturalist 的工作人员一起在《自然生态与进化》上发表了一篇评论文章，概述了这些数据库如何被人工智能生成的数据伪造和公共错误信息“污染”。

柳树山雀是一个极端的例子——整个动物完全由代码生成——据利斯说，它几乎足以欺骗一些“鸟类学家”。 但人工智能不需要创建完整的观察结果来污染科学记录——增强也可能会出现问题。

“与试图将完全由人工智能生成的图像冒充为生物记录的人相比，现有图像的去噪和‘美化’问题可能要普遍得多，但两者都存在很大的问题，”利斯说。

在他们的论文中，利斯和他的团队展示了生成赝品是多么容易。 他们要求 Google 支持的聊天机器人 Gemini 生成一张红翼黑鸟站在蓝天树枝上的图像。 除了尾羽数量看起来很奇怪之外，结果相当令人信服。

他们还拍了一张原产于南美的黄莺的照片，并要求双子座“让这张照片看起来更好”。 人工智能制作的图像似乎为黄莺的翅膀添加了红色耀斑，这使得研究小组认为它可能会欺骗鸟类学家或计算机视觉分类器，将其视为红翅黑鸟的真实例子。

最近，iNaturalist 上无意中发生了这种情况。 一位用户以同样的方式修改了图像，从而产生了对巴西红翅黑鸟的第一个描述。 这已被检测到，并且该图像已从数据库中隐藏。

恶作剧的历史

查尔顿硫磺的翅膀在阳光下闪烁着鲜艳的黄色，只有两个大胆的蓝色月亮，每个翅膀上都有一个。 1700 年代初，伦敦化学家詹姆斯·佩蒂弗 (James Petiver) 的朋友威廉·查尔顿 (William Charlton) 送给他这种壮观的鳞翅目昆虫，并首次描述了这种蝴蝶。

到 1763 年，该物种已进入科学文献，作为现代生物分类之父卡尔·林奈 (Carl Linnaeus) 撰写的《Centuria Insectorum Rariorum》中列出的 100 种无脊椎动物之一。

交给佩蒂弗的标本在整个 18 世纪一直保存在大英博物馆，直到丹麦昆虫专家约翰·克里斯蒂安·法布里修斯 (Johann Christian Fabricius) 对它进行了检查。 法布里修斯指出，翅膀上的两个蓝色月亮并不是一个物种长期进化的标志。

它们是人类双手在普通硫磺翅膀上留下的痕迹。 查尔顿硫磺并不存在。

虽然目前还不清楚这是否是一次故意的欺骗（有报道称，大英博物馆的一位馆长对假货非常愤怒，以至于将其踩成了灰尘）还是一个简单的恶作剧，但它突显了恶作剧长期以来一直是识别和检查物种的一部分，以及它们对科学记录的影响。

澳大利亚生活地图集 (ALA) 的发言人表示：“数据质量是生物多样性数据中的一个问题，早于电子数据甚至计算机，更不用说人工智能了。” ALA 是一个数字化、开放的基础设施，汇集了来自全国各地的生物多样性数据——有时神话和奇幻的数据已经溜进了数据库。

“像大多数数据管理人员一样，《澳大利亚生活地图集》中提交了相当多的独角兽、霸王龙和匿名恋人，但这些都已被过滤掉。”

人工智能是力量倍增器。 生成工具使此类伪造变得简单。 任何有时间的人都可以轻松使用这些工具。 在社交媒体上，假物种迅速扩散，通常还伴随着人工智能生成的关于其行为和栖息地的描述。 通常，人们的反应是轻信的，相信图像是真实的。

间谍社区

虽然公民科学平台很容易受到人工智能生成的提交内容的影响，但他们的社区充满了忠诚而诚实的贡献者，他们追随自己的热情或寻求做出改变。 这些成员具有敏锐的洞察力和奉献精神。

“有很多真正有能力的审阅者和贡献者，他们投入了大量的时间来维护数据库的完整性，”利斯说。 “我怀疑我们需要工具包来标记可能有问题的记录，”他补充道。

对于拥有约 5 亿张图像的 iNaturalist 来说，假货的威胁并不新鲜。 它一直在与 Photoshop 图像和使用从互联网其他地方获得的图像的错误记录进行斗争。 一切都在快速发展，iNaturist 知道它也必须快速发展。

iNaturalist 发言人告诉 Particle：“随着人工智能工具变得越来越容易使用以及技术格局发生变化，我们正在努力适应，同时将科学完整性作为我们工作的核心。”

为了打击人工智能生成的欺诈行为，发言人指出，最近添加了标记人工智能生成内容的社区工具，以维护 iNaturalist 上生物多样性数据的可靠性。

螳螂专家安德森坚信，科学文献最终将经历人工智能造假的案例。 利斯对此表示同意，他说“声称有一项发现是很容易的”，并暗示，如果科学家故意进行这种欺骗，那么这肯定是一种不当行为和欺诈。

“我们希望这不会发生，”利斯说。

生态学家、自然资源保护主义者和公民科学平台正在经历生成式人工智能的兴起以及气候变化和生物多样性丧失的双重危机，这令人深感担忧。 但第三场危机涉及分类学——物种分类的科学。 没有足够的专家来描述和编目物种。

虽然失控的生成式人工智能列车尚未陷入这三重危机，但不难想象，不断改进的人工智能图像模型很快就会在现实与幻想之间产生如此难以察觉的区别，即使是最有洞察力的专家也很难区分。 我们如何反击？

对策

Lees 认为，可以从三个方面来应对人工智能在这些领域的崛起。 他们建议公民科学平台应该拥有强大的图像验证协议和元数据检查，以确保上传的图像是合法的观察结果。

更重要的是确保那些使用人工智能工具和公民科学平台的人意识到他们所使用的系统的陷阱。 “鉴于问题的很大一部分是公众采用新技术，因此有关由此引起的问题的教育有望有所帮助，”利斯说。

尽管人们强烈希望将人工智能排除在公民科学平台之外，但在某些情况下，人工智能和机器学习模型可能有利于保护和生物多样性工作。 ALA 发言人表示：“人工智能带来了新的挑战，但也带来了潜在的新解决方案。”

利用 eBird 数据，人工智能模型在鸟类迁徙前几周就预测了鸟类的迁徙模式。 CitClops 项目是一个公民科学项目，要求公众拍摄海水照片，利用人工智能来监测藻华的早期迹象。

在澳大利亚，机器学习系统的工作方式与制造假货的生成式人工智能系统不同，最近被澳大利亚野生动物保护协会用来解读相机陷阱中的图像。 该人工智能已经接受了超过 110 万张野生动物图像的训练（这些图像也经过了真人的审查）。 这使得它能够识别出鸸鹋或小袋鼠等动物，从而大大减少了检查相机陷阱的体力劳动。 值得注意的是，物种分类并不是人工智能的职责。 人工智能帮助将图像分组到数据集中，并由人类验证工作。

正是这个元素——我们——似乎是我们对生成人工智能带来的错误信息和伪造爆炸式增长进行抵抗的关键。 迄今为止，事实证明，公民科学平台的热情和奉献的贡献者和管理者是抵御斜坡入侵的最佳防御手段。
